__inputs.name: DS_PROMETHEUS
__inputs.label: Prometheus
__inputs.description: Prometheus data source scraping the orleans.lattice (and optionally orleans.lattice.replication) meter.

panels.title: Dependency wait p95 (ms) - causal-consistency staging
panels.description: Wait time for entries parked in the causal-apply buffer awaiting dependency satisfaction. Only emits samples when causal staging is enabled AND at least one entry parks. Flat-zero (no series) is the healthy steady state - the 'or vector(0)' guard renders zero rather than 'No data'.

panels.title: Dead-letter queue churn (ops/s)
panels.description: Dead-letter enqueue/removal rate. Only emits when permanent transport or apply failures occur. Flat-zero is the healthy steady state.

panels.title: Apply correctness violations (rate)
panels.description: FIFO and causal-violation counters. A sustained nonzero rate indicates a real correctness regression. Flat-zero is required for a healthy cluster.

panels.title: Peer fell-off-log events (count over range)
panels.description: Receiver fell-off-log detections per peer. Nonzero means the receiver's high-water-mark is older than the sender's oldest WAL entry - i.e. the receiver missed the catch-up window. Flat-zero is the healthy steady state.

panels.title: Apply buffer (entries)
panels.description: Causal-apply buffer occupancy in entries. Only emits when causal staging parks an entry. Flat-zero (or absent) means no causal staging is engaged. When non-zero, see the apply-lag overlay panel for the bistability signal. The matching bytes panel is rendered to the right of this one.

panels.title: Per-peer last outbound ship (seconds ago)
panels.description: Wall-clock seconds since the local sender last successfully shipped a batch (or an empty liveness probe) to the named peer. Filters on direction=outbound; the inbound twin panel renders the receiver-side timeline.

panels.title: Apply lag p99 vs apply-buffer depth (causal-staging bistability overlay)
panels.description: Overlays apply-lag p99 (left axis, ms) against the causal-apply buffer occupancy (right axis, entries). The bistability hypothesis: once the buffer crosses ~N entries, apply-lag p99 stays pegged at a high level for the rest of the window even as the buffer eventually drains. If only the lag panel renders (buffer flat-zero), causal staging is not engaged and the bistability is in a different layer (e.g. shipper backpressure, sender-side WAL). Use this panel as the first stop when the lag-p99 sweep shows wide run-to-run variance.

panels.title: Apply buffer (bytes)
panels.description: Causal-apply buffer occupancy in bytes. Tracks the same lifecycle as the entries panel to its left at byte granularity. Together they bound the buffer against CausalBufferMaxEntries and CausalBufferMaxBytes. Flat-zero (or absent) means no causal staging is engaged.

panels.title: Per-peer bytes behind
panels.description: Cumulative WAL payload bytes the local sender has yet to ship to each peer. Companion to the per-peer entries-behind panel to the left.

panels.title: Per-peer last inbound apply (seconds ago)
panels.description: Wall-clock seconds since the local receiver last successfully applied a batch authored by the named peer. Filters on direction=inbound; symmetric twin of the outbound ship panel.

panels.title: Per-peer negotiated wire version
panels.description: Framing wire version the local sender has negotiated as the target for the named peer (min(localCurrent, peerAdvertised), or the unknown-peer floor until the peer advertises). Capability/telemetry only - the sender does not yet re-encode at this version (see follow-up issue).

panels.title: Per-peer wire-version downgrade active (1 = mixed-version fleet)
panels.description: 1 when the negotiated target version is strictly below the sender's current wire version (a mixed-version fleet during a rolling upgrade), else 0. Telemetry only - reflects the negotiated target, not an actual re-encode.

panels.title: Anti-entropy digest-probe comparisons (rate, by outcome)
panels.description: Per-shard digest comparisons performed by the anti-entropy probe scheduler, by outcome (match / mismatch / version_skew / remote_unavailable). Dark/opt-in: zero unless DigestProbeEnabled is set.

panels.title: Anti-entropy digest divergence (mismatch rate)
panels.description: Per-shard digest comparisons whose versions matched but hashes differed - the local cluster and the named peer have diverged for that shard. Pair with the comparisons panel to compute the divergence ratio. Dark/opt-in.

panels.title: Redundant payload re-send rate
panels.description: Rate of byte-identical content re-sets the shipper observed while content-hash dedup measurement is enabled (ContentHashDedupEnabled). 'entries/s' counts redundant Set entries; 'bytes/s' is the value bytes they carried. Flat-zero unless the workload re-sets identical values for a key. Observability-only - the shipper never elides or reorders bytes on the wire.

panels.title: Effective ship batch size (adaptive)
panels.description: Per-tick outbound batch cap the shipper actually used, distribution p50/p95/p99. With adaptive sizing on (AdaptiveBatchSizingEnabled=true, the default) the AIMD controller keeps it at the configured ShipBatchSize on a healthy link and backs it off on rising ack latency or send errors, so a sustained dip flags a degraded peer or repeated apply failures; with it off it sits flat at ShipBatchSize. The receiver flow-control hint is always the hard ceiling.

panels.title: Ship ack latency p50/p95/p99 (ms)
panels.description: Round-trip latency from sending a batch to receiving its ack, per (tree, peer). This is the primary signal the adaptive batch-size controller reacts to: a sustained rise above AdaptiveBatchLatencyThreshold shrinks the effective batch size. Emitted on every acknowledged batch regardless of whether adaptive sizing is enabled.

panels.title: Merkle-walk leaves localised (rate)
panels.description: Rate of diverging leaves the read-only anti-entropy Merkle walk narrowed a shard mismatch down to. Opt-in via MerkleWalkEnabled; stays zero unless a range-answering probe transport is wired up.

panels.title: Merkle-walk aborted (rate by reason)
panels.description: Rate of read-only Merkle-walk passes that stopped before localising, split by reason (depth_cap, byte_budget, remote_unavailable, version_skew). With the default transport every triggered walk reports remote_unavailable.

panels.title: Pre-ship coalescing elided rate
panels.description: Rate of redundant per-key versions the shipper dropped from outbound batches by pre-ship coalescing (PreShipCoalescingEnabled, last-writer-wins trees only). 'entries/s' counts elided WAL entries; 'bytes/s' is the pre-encoded wire-segment bytes they carried. Flat-zero unless a hot key is rewritten several times within one ship window. The coalesced output is a strict subset an unmodified receiver converges to identically.

panels.title: Leaf re-replay entries re-shipped (rate)
panels.description: Rate of retained write-ahead-log entries the targeted leaf re-replay repair stage re-shipped to a diverged peer. Opt-in via LeafReReplayEnabled; stays zero unless localisation finds a divergent leaf and a real push transport is wired up.

panels.title: Leaf re-replay skipped (rate by reason)
panels.description: Rate of targeted leaf re-replay passes that skipped without re-shipping, split by reason (disabled, range_empty, wal_trimmed). A wal_trimmed series is the operator-only alert: the local WAL was garbage-collected past the divergence point and a bootstrap-snapshot remediation is required.

panels.title: Apply parallelism - runs per batch
panels.description: Distribution of the receiver apply degree-of-parallelism chosen per batch (orleans.lattice.replication.apply.parallel_runs). 1 = serial apply (the default, or a batch with no independent (tree, origin) runs); higher values appear only when ApplyMaxParallelRuns > 1 and the batch fans out across independent runs.

panels.title: Outbound batches in flight per peer
panels.description: Current count of shipped-but-unacknowledged replication batches per peer (orleans.lattice.replication.peer.ship_in_flight observable gauge). Climbs toward ShipMaxInFlight when pipelining is enabled and the peer is the bottleneck; flat at 0 or 1 with default settings.

panels.title: Bootstrap throughput (rate)
panels.description: Per-tree rate of entries and value bytes received by the receiver bootstrap/backfill path (orleans.lattice.replication.bootstrap.entries_received / bootstrap.bytes_received). Non-zero only while a peer is catching up a cold or fell-off-log receiver.

panels.title: Bootstrap duration p50/p95/p99 (ms)
panels.description: Wall-clock duration of receiver bootstrap operations (orleans.lattice.replication.bootstrap.duration), tagged by origin and outcome. Long tails indicate large backfills or a slow source.

panels.title: Bootstrap transient retries (rate)
panels.description: Rate of transient (retryable) failures during receiver bootstrap (orleans.lattice.replication.bootstrap.transient_retries), by tree. A sustained non-zero rate signals a flaky source link slowing convergence.

panels.title: Fall-off-log suppressed events (rate)
panels.description: Rate of fall-off-log detections suppressed as duplicates (orleans.lattice.replication.peer.fell_off_log_suppressed), by tree. Pairs with the peer.fell_off_log panel: a high suppressed-to-raised ratio means the detector is correctly de-duplicating repeated signals for the same gap.

panels.title: Bootstrap fallback triggered (rate)
panels.description: Rate of scoped bootstrap-snapshot fallback passes that began after a targeted leaf re-replay reported the local write-ahead-log was garbage-collected past the divergence point. Opt-in via BootstrapFallbackEnabled; stays zero unless a wal_trimmed leaf re-replay occurs and the fallback is enabled.

panels.title: Bootstrap fallback entries re-shipped (rate)
panels.description: Rate of committed-projection entries the scoped bootstrap-snapshot fallback re-derived from the live tree and re-shipped to a diverged peer. Opt-in via BootstrapFallbackEnabled; stays zero unless a fallback pass ships at least one entry.

panels.title: Bootstrap fallback skipped (rate by reason)
panels.description: Rate of scoped bootstrap-snapshot fallback passes that skipped without re-shipping, split by reason (disabled, range_empty, empty). A disabled series is the operator-only signal that a wal_trimmed divergence was repairable but the fallback was not opted in.

panels.title: Remediation disabled (tree/peer by reason)
panels.description: Each (tree, peer) for which automatic anti-entropy remediation is currently disabled, valued 1 and split by reason (opt_out, budget_exhausted, circuit_open). opt_out is the steady-state signal that drift was localised but the host has not set AutoRemediateOnDigestMismatch; budget_exhausted means the per-window remediation traffic budget is spent; circuit_open means the per-tree/peer circuit breaker tripped on consecutive failures. No series means remediation is permitted.

panels.title: Remediation skipped (rate by reason)
panels.description: Rate of automatic anti-entropy remediation passes skipped before sending any repair traffic, split by reason (opt_out, budget_exhausted, circuit_open). The drift was still detected and probed; only the repair action was suppressed. Stays at the opt_out rate until AutoRemediateOnDigestMismatch is enabled.

panels.title: Shared-dictionary compression ratio
panels.description: Achieved shared-dictionary Zstandard compression ratio on the framing encode path (FramingCompression = ZstdDictionary with a non-zero FramingCompressionDictionaryId). 'ratio' is compressed-out over uncompressed-in (lower is better; 1.0 means no saving); 'in bytes/s' and 'out bytes/s' are the before/after byte rates. Flat-zero unless shared-dictionary compression is opted into and a dictionary resolves on this silo.

panels.title: Content-hash payload elision (rate)
panels.description: Rate of Set-entry payloads and value bytes elided from outbound batches by the sender-manifest / receiver-pull-missing content-hash round trip (orleans.lattice.replication.ship.elided_payloads / ship.elided_payload_bytes). Opt-in via ContentHashDedupElisionEnabled (which also requires ContentHashDedupEnabled); flat-zero unless elision is enabled and a peer advertises the exchange capability for a duplicate-heavy workload.

panels.title: Content-hash manifest exchanges (rate)
panels.description: Rate of content-hash manifest exchanges performed with each peer on the outbound ship path (orleans.lattice.replication.ship.manifest_exchanges). One per shipped batch that advertised a manifest. Read alongside the elision panel to gauge average payloads elided per exchange and whether the pull-missing round trip is paying for itself.

panels.title: Pre-ship CRDT deltas merged (rate)
panels.description: Rate of source CRDT deltas the shipper folded into a combined delta by pre-ship coalescing (PreShipCoalescingEnabled, recognised CRDT trees). 'deltas/s' counts the same-key typed deltas merged into one combined-delta entry; pairs with the coalesce entries-elided panel which records the source entries dropped from the wire. Flat-zero unless a hot CRDT key is mutated several times within one ship window, or the tree is last-writer-wins (which elides entries without merging deltas).

panels.title: Shared-dictionary negotiation outcomes (rate)
panels.description: Rate of per-peer shared-dictionary capability negotiations by outcome (orleans.lattice.replication.ship.dictionary_negotiation). matched = the peer advertised the configured dictionary id and the sender compressed with it; fell_back = the peer advertised a capability without the configured id; unknown = the peer has not advertised a dictionary capability yet. Opt-in via DictionaryNegotiationEnabled with a ZstdDictionary tree; flat-zero unless negotiation is enabled and a shared dictionary is configured.

targets.expr: sum by (tree, peer, outcome) (rate(orleans_lattice_replication_ship_dictionary_negotiation_total{tree=~"$tree",peer=~"$peer",cluster=~"$cluster",instance=~"$silo"}[5m])) or vector(0)

panels.title: Batches shipped with vs without a shared dictionary (rate)
panels.description: Rate of batches shipped on the dictionary-eligible path split by whether a shared dictionary was used (orleans.lattice.replication.ship.dictionary_batches). with_dictionary = compressed against a negotiated shared dictionary; without_dictionary = plain dictionary-less Zstd (the fallback for a peer that has not advertised the configured id). Read alongside the negotiation-outcomes panel to confirm a mixed fleet keeps shipping during a rolling dictionary rollout.

targets.expr: sum by (tree, peer, dictionary) (rate(orleans_lattice_replication_ship_dictionary_batches_total{tree=~"$tree",peer=~"$peer",cluster=~"$cluster",instance=~"$silo"}[5m])) or vector(0)

panels.title: Receiver content-hash exchanges handled (rate)
panels.description: Rate of content-hash manifest exchanges the receiver answered for each origin peer (orleans.lattice.replication.receiver.content_manifest_exchanges). One per inbound pull-missing request handled. Pairs with the sender-side manifest-exchanges panel so an operator can confirm both ends of the round trip agree on the exchange volume. Flat-zero unless a peer ships with ContentHashDedupElisionEnabled against this receiver.

panels.title: Receiver content entries elided (rate)
panels.description: Rate of manifest entries the receiver reported it already holds byte-identical content for (orleans.lattice.replication.receiver.content_entries_elided) - the entries the receiver told the sender it does not need shipped. Pairs with the sender-side content-hash payload elision panel: the two track the same elided entries from each end of the round trip. Flat-zero unless the receiver's applied-content index is populated (ContentHashDedupEnabled) and a peer advertises the exchange.

panels.title: Receiver metadata-only HWM advances (rate)
panels.description: Rate of metadata-only per-origin high-water-mark advances the receiver performed during a content-hash exchange (orleans.lattice.replication.receiver.content_hwm_advances) - the identical-content-newer-clock idempotent re-set case where the high-water-mark advances without the payload travelling. Flat-zero unless idempotent upstream retry re-sends byte-identical content with a newer clock and the receiver already holds it.

panels.title: Shared-dictionary convergence pulls (rate)
panels.description: Rate of shared-dictionary convergence byte-pulls a sender performed against an advertising peer (orleans.lattice.replication.ship.dictionary_convergence), tagged by outcome. installed = the peer served the advertised dictionary bytes and the sender installed them (fingerprint-verified); rejected = the peer served bytes whose fingerprint did not match the advertisement, so they were discarded; unavailable = the peer or transport did not serve the bytes (un-upgraded peer, transport fallback). Opt-in via AddLatticeAutoSharedDictionary; flat-zero unless the self-distributing auto-dictionary feature is enabled and a peer advertises a dictionary this sender does not yet hold.

targets.expr: sum by (tree, peer, outcome) (rate(orleans_lattice_replication_ship_dictionary_convergence_total{tree=~"$tree",peer=~"$peer",cluster=~"$cluster",instance=~"$silo"}[5m])) or vector(0)

panels.title: Wire-version down-stamp outcomes (rate by reason)
panels.description: Rate of per-batch wire-version down-stamp outcomes the shipper recorded while negotiating the framing version for an older peer (orleans.lattice.replication.ship.wire_version_down_stamp), split by reason. compression_dropped = a last-writer-wins tree's framing compression was auto-dropped for this peer so it keeps replicating uncompressed (lossless); blocked_crdt_mode = a CRDT-mode tree cannot be faithfully down-encoded for a pre-current-version receiver, so replication to the peer is paused until upgrade; blocked_unsupported_version = the negotiated target is below the down-encode floor. Opt-in via WireVersionNegotiationEnabled; flat-zero unless a mixed-version fleet is down-stamping. A non-zero blocked_* series is the operator-actionable signal that a peer must be upgraded.

targets.expr: sum by (tree, peer, reason) (rate(orleans_lattice_replication_ship_wire_version_down_stamp_total{tree=~"$tree",peer=~"$peer",cluster=~"$cluster",instance=~"$silo"}[5m])) or vector(0)

panels.title: Log-tailing producer: leaf WAL append vs ship rate (ops/s)
panels.description: Throughput of the log-first replication producer. appended = entries committed to the leaf write-ahead log by WalCommitLogWriter (orleans.lattice.wal.shard.dispatch.entries), which is now the sole appender; the replication sink no longer performs a redundant second WAL append. shipped = entries the shipper drained from that same WAL and sent to peers (orleans.lattice.replication.wal.entries_shipped). In steady state the two series track each other; a sustained gap (appended outpacing shipped) is the log-tailing producer falling behind the WAL it tails - cross-check with per-peer entries-behind and fell-off-log.

panels.title: Shipper doorbell coalescing (rate)
panels.description: Rate of commit-time shipper-doorbell rings, split by whether each ring reached the shipper or was coalesced at the source. 'rung/s' (orleans.lattice.replication.doorbell.rung) counts rings actually dispatched to the non-reentrant shipper activation (the in-flight ring plus any trailing follow-up); 'coalesced/s' (orleans.lattice.replication.doorbell.coalesced) counts per-commit ring requests folded into the single pending follow-up because a ring for the same (tree, peer) was already in flight. Both fire when ShipDoorbellEnabled is true (the default). Under a sustained write burst 'coalesced/s' dominates while 'rung/s' stays near the small constant the shipper needs to stay awake - a high coalesced-to-rung ratio is the storm the coalescer is absorbing, keeping the shipper's turn queue from blowing up. A near-zero coalesced/s with rung/s tracking the commit rate means writes arrive slower than the shipper drains - no storm to absorb.

panels.title: Coordinated restore: saga phase and write-fence durations (p95, ms)
panels.description: 95th-percentile duration of coordinated multi-cluster restore saga phases and per-tree write-fence windows. 'phase p95' (orleans.lattice.replication.saga.phase.duration, split by phase = prepare/commit/abort) separates the long unfenced prepare (shadow build) window from the short fenced cutover. 'fence p95' (orleans.lattice.replication.saga.fence.duration, per tree) measures only the write-blocking cutover window (engage to lift), NOT the longer globally-gated shipping pause - so a fence duration that grows toward the whole build window is the operator-actionable signal that a cutover is not staying bounded.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, phase) (rate(orleans_lattice_replication_saga_phase_duration_milliseconds_bucket{cluster=~"$cluster",instance=~"$silo"}[5m]))) or vector(0)
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, tree) (rate(orleans_lattice_replication_saga_fence_duration_milliseconds_bucket{tree=~"$tree",cluster=~"$cluster",instance=~"$silo"}[5m]))) or vector(0)

panels.title: Coordinated restore: participant votes, commits and aborts (rate)
panels.description: Rate of coordinated-restore participant outcomes. 'vote' (orleans.lattice.replication.saga.participant.votes, split by reason) counts prepare votes: commit, or an abort reason (infeasible = admission refused a target that cannot fit; precondition = a missing backup/base in the manifest chain; build-failed = the bounded build-retry budget was exhausted; engine-unavailable = the backup package is not wired here; not-replicated = the saga named a target tree this cluster does not replicate and was refused). 'commit' (orleans.lattice.replication.saga.participant.commits) and 'abort' (orleans.lattice.replication.saga.participant.aborts) count terminal cutovers and rollbacks. A rising abort/vote fraction, or a spike in a specific abort reason, is the operator signal that restores are failing admission or build.

panels.title: Coordinated restore: saga compensations (rate by cause)
panels.description: Rate of coordinated-restore compensations (rollbacks), split by cause (orleans.lattice.replication.saga.compensations). vote-abort = a coordinator-driven rollback after at least one participant voted abort (an all-or-nothing rollback of every prepared cluster); coordinator-loss = a participant's own cutover-fence-expiry auto-compensation after the coordinator decision never arrived. A non-zero coordinator-loss series is the operator-actionable signal that a coordinator cluster is being lost mid-saga and the bounded fence timer is the only thing preventing a leaked prepared restore.

panels.title: WAL GC pass rate by outcome (ops/s)
panels.description: Rate of WAL garbage-collection passes the per-silo scheduler drove, split by outcome (orleans.lattice.wal.gc.passes). reclaimed = the pass trimmed at least one entry, so the tree had backlog above the trim floor; blocked = the pass reclaimed nothing in at least one WAL partition because no durable leaf-materialiser pin carried a usable offset there, so that partition's consumer-cursor branch was disabled and it CANNOT reclaim at all; no_consumer = no consumer has reported a cursor, so there was no frontier to trim against and the WAL cannot shrink; idle = the pass evaluated a usable floor and simply found nothing above it, which is the healthy quiet state; unclassified = a cursor-floor state this build does not name, expected to read a permanent zero; failed = the pass threw. ONLY reclaimed is an affirmative reading: every other arm means nothing was trimmed, so blocked = 0 on its own is not evidence of reclamation - a tree parked forever on no_consumer satisfies it too. The blocked value was split out of idle by issue #2702: the two are opposite conditions - one strands WAL without bound, the other has nothing to do - and until then they were indistinguishable here, on a deployment that carried both simultaneously. no_consumer and unclassified were split out of idle by issue #2850 for the same reason, because idle was still a catch-all absorbing a tree that could not evaluate a floor at all. Since issue #2849 the block is scoped to the partitions an unusable pin actually covers, so a partially blocked tree can trim its healthy partitions and appear here as reclaimed on the same pass; the blocked-leaf remedy and the cadence floor read the pass report's cursor-floor state directly rather than this tag, so neither is weakened by that. Emitted once per pass unconditionally, and additionally zero-primed per tree for EVERY outcome arm (issue #2774), so each series survives a return to zero rather than vanishing when a tree recovers, and an absent arm is a reporting failure rather than a healthy reading. That is why this panel carries no 'or vector(0)' compensation: the compensation would render a missing series as a flat zero, which is the exact ambiguity the priming removes, so keeping both would re-create the fault behind something that looks like a fix. A missing line here means the build did not land. This is the denominator for the per-tree reclaim rate and the reference that tells apart a tree with no backlog from a tree that is not being collected at all.

panels.title: WAL GC adaptive interval (p50/p95, s)
panels.description: The cadence the WAL garbage-collection scheduler selected per tree after its most recent pass (orleans.lattice.wal.gc.interval). The value moves inside the configured band [LatticeOptions.WalGcMinInterval, LatticeOptions.WalGcInterval], and a reading at the ceiling is a quiet tree. A sustained reading at the FLOOR now has two causes and they are not interchangeable: a tree whose log is growing faster than one pass reclaims, which is working as intended, or a tree held at the floor because it is blocked from reclaiming at all (issue #2702), which is a fault. The pass-outcome panel beside this one separates them - pair a floor reading with a non-zero blocked rate to identify the second. Read against that panel this shows the cadence tightening under backlog and relaxing once the backlog clears.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.5, sum by (le, tree) (rate(orleans_lattice_wal_gc_interval_seconds_bucket{tree=~"$tree",cluster=~"$cluster",instance=~"$silo"}[5m]))) or vector(0)
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, tree) (rate(orleans_lattice_wal_gc_interval_seconds_bucket{tree=~"$tree",cluster=~"$cluster",instance=~"$silo"}[5m]))) or vector(0)

panels.title: WAL GC retained backlog after pass (p95, bytes)
panels.description: 95th-percentile retained WAL bytes left after a garbage-collection pass (orleans.lattice.wal.gc.backlog_bytes), sampled from the pass own report so it costs no extra I/O. Byte accounting is a provider capability gated behind LatticeOptions.WalMaxRetainedBytes, so this series is absent on a host without it. Do NOT infer the reason from the absence: orleans.lattice.wal.gc.backlog_bytes_unavailable is emitted on any pass that could not sample, tagged with the reason (policy_disabled or provider_unsupported), and the panel beside it reads it directly (issue #2694).

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, tree) (rate(orleans_lattice_wal_gc_backlog_bytes_bucket{tree=~"$tree",cluster=~"$cluster",instance=~"$silo"}[5m]))) or vector(0)

panels.title: WAL GC backlog bytes unavailable by reason (ops/s) - issue #2694
panels.description: Rate of WAL garbage-collection passes that could NOT sample the retained-backlog histogram beside this panel (orleans.lattice.wal.gc.backlog_bytes_unavailable), tagged by reason: policy_disabled means the pass computed no byte ceiling, so LatticeOptions.WalMaxRetainedBytes is unset - the default configuration, and an expected steady rate rather than a fault; provider_unsupported means a ceiling was computed but the IWalStorageProvider reports no byte accounting, which IS a misconfiguration because the operator asked for a byte policy the provider cannot enforce. This panel exists because the backlog histogram is silent in exactly the configuration most deployments run, and silence looks identical whether the policy is off, the provider cannot count, or the collector is wedged. With this series the first two announce themselves and name their reason, so only genuine silence remains unexplained.

panels.title: WAL GC offset floor unavailable (ops/s)
panels.description: Rate of WAL garbage-collection passes that could not compute the durable leaf-materialiser offset floor because the pin-store read threw, so the pass fell back to no offset floor (orleans.lattice.wal.gc.offset_floor_unavailable). The fallback is safe for a single pass because the HLC floor still constrains the trim, but the failure was otherwise silent (issue #2314): a persistently unreachable pin store removes the offset floor on every pass indefinitely, indistinguishable from a tree that legitimately has no offset floor. The healthy no-floor outcomes - no durable pin store wired, or a reachable store reporting no offsets - do not reach this catch and do not increment the counter, so a sustained non-zero rate here means the offset floor is not being applied and the low-HLC/high-offset reap class it retains is protected only by the HLC floor until the store recovers. Read against the pass-outcome panel: a tree collecting normally but ticking this series is losing its offset floor.

panels.title: WAL GC blocked passes by tree (ops/s) - issue #2702
panels.description: Rate of WAL garbage-collection passes that reclaimed nothing because no durable leaf-materialiser pin carried a usable offset, so the consumer-cursor branch was disabled for at least one WAL partition (orleans.lattice.wal.gc.passes, outcome=blocked). This is NOT the quiet tree that outcome=idle describes: a blocked partition cannot reclaim at all and its WAL grows without bound, whereas an idle tree simply has nothing above the trim floor. The two shared the idle label until issue #2702, and because the same observation also drove the scheduler's backoff, a blocked tree was relaxed toward LatticeOptions.WalGcInterval exactly like a quiet one - the tree needing the most frequent passes received the fewest, self-reinforcingly. A blocked tree is now held at LatticeOptions.WalGcMinInterval instead, so this panel's companion reading is the adaptive-interval panel pinned at the floor. Since issue #2849 the block is scoped to the partitions the unusable pin covers rather than the whole tree, so a tree can appear on this series while its healthy partitions reclaim; the tree is still held at the cadence floor and still names its blocking consumer on the paired warning log. Read it two ways: a sustained non-zero rate is a tree stranding WAL it cannot release, and a rate that falls to zero AND STAYS THERE is a repair that held - but note that this series falling to zero is by itself only the absence of one named failure, not evidence of reclamation; pair it with outcome=reclaimed rising, which is the only affirmative arm. The series is deliberately zero-primed once per tree by the scheduler, so a tree that has never blocked reports a real zero rather than no series, and a tree that recovers keeps reporting zero rather than disappearing at exactly the moment a reader is confirming the recovery. For that reason this query intentionally omits the 'or vector(0)' fallback used elsewhere on this dashboard: fabricating a zero for an absent series would reintroduce the false zero the priming exists to remove, and here an absent series genuinely means the scheduler is not running on the selected silo.

panels.title: WAL GC blocked-leaf reactivations by outcome (ops/s) - issue #2710
panels.description: Reactivations of a dormant leaf whose durable materialiser pin was blocking its tree's WAL cursor floor (orleans.lattice.wal.gc.blocked_leaf_reactivations, issue #2710 Limitation 2). Read it against the blocked-passes panel beside it: that panel is the condition, this one is the remedy acting on it. A blocking consumer is by construction one whose leaf is NOT activated, because the floor skips every consumer present in the live cursor registry before it evaluates the pin - so no leaf-local trigger can reach this population and the retention path has to be the one to touch it. attempted = the scheduler reactivated a named blocking leaf, rate-limited by a minimum block age, a retry cooldown and a hard attempt budget; healed = a previously-touched consumer stopped blocking, which is evidence the sweep is working rather than proof it caused the heal, since ordinary traffic could have touched the leaf first; abandoned = a consumer stayed blocked across every permitted attempt OF A CYCLE; rearmed = an abandoned consumer's attempt budget was restored after a backoff (issue #2783); undelivered = the touch was issued but the grain call did not return within its budget (issue #2768); completed = the leaf was resolved and touched without error, which is a statement about the TOUCH and not about the pin; unresolvable = the blocking consumer id did not resolve to a leaf at all, so nothing was touched, and because that is a permanent property of the id it still consumes budget; faulted = the touch was issued and threw, which is evidence about the silo rather than about the leaf and is refundable in the same way undelivered is; and five DRIVE arms added by issue #2692 - drove_lifted, drove_no_advance, drove_memory_refused, drove_not_driven and drove_already_driving - plus drove_timed_out added by issue #3065 - which record what the touch ACHIEVED rather than merely that it was issued, and which are charted with their full interpretation on the starved-leaf drive panel below. This panel carries no outcome matcher, so it charts all fourteen arms by construction and any arm added later appears here without an edit. COMPLETED IS NOT HEALED AND THE GAP BETWEEN THEM IS A READING IN ITS OWN RIGHT (issue #2938): completed says the sweep reached the leaf, healed says the pin subsequently cleared, so completed advancing while healed stays flat means reachability was achieved and was NOT SUFFICIENT to clear the pin - a second defect downstream of the delivery problem rather than the delivery problem persisting. ABANDONED IS THE ALARM: it means the block is not clearable by activation alone, so the leaf's snapshot capture is failing for a separate reason - an oversized leaf that cannot be serialised is the known case - and the WAL stays retained until that is fixed. UNDELIVERED IS NOT ABANDONED AND MUST NOT BE READ AS IT: abandoned means the leaf was reached and stayed blocked, undelivered means it was never reached at all, so a sweep whose touches all time out reads as undelivered rather than masquerading as a leaf that cannot be healed. Read abandoned against rearmed: the two advancing in step is a hopeless tree retrying on an ever-slower schedule, which is the designed shape, whereas abandoned advancing while rearmed stays flat means the sweep has genuinely stopped. All fourteen outcomes share one instrument and EVERY ONE IS ZERO-PRIMED per tree on every GC pass, above every early return, so a zero on healed is a measured zero rather than an unpublished series and an absent series means the build carrying the sweep never landed - which is what lets a reader tell a sweep that ran without effect from one that was never reached. READING A FLAT ZERO AS THE OUTCOME NEVER OCCURRED DEPENDS ON TWO SEPARATE CONDITIONS AND PRIMING IS ONLY THE FIRST. The arm has to exist at all - until issue #2938 three of the four terminal outcomes had no arm of their own, so their occurrences were counted on no series while this description said all five and the code could already produce eight - and the arm has to be reachable on the recording path (issue #2942), because an armed tag value whose emission site can never execute primes at zero and is indistinguishable from one that genuinely did not occur. Both conditions are held by fixtures rather than by review: exhaustive arming by an enum-driven gate, reachability by an identity matrix that induces each outcome in turn and asserts it lands on its own arm and on no other. The query therefore needs no 'or vector(0)' fallback: the zeros are real observations minted by a pass that demonstrably ran, not fabricated ones. The blocking leaf is named on the paired warning log rather than as a tag here, because the leaf population is unbounded and would be an unbounded metric dimension.

panels.title: WAL GC blocked-leaf sweep abandon/re-arm totals over range - issue #2783
panels.description: Totals (not a rate) of the abandonment, re-arm, undelivered, completed, faulted, unresolvable and orphaned arms of orleans.lattice.wal.gc.blocked_leaf_reactivations over the selected range, per tree. This is deliberately a totals panel rather than a second rate panel: once a tree has been abandoned its retries back off to hours apart, so its re-arm cadence falls far below the resolution of the 5 m rate window used by the panel beside it and would render as a flat zero there. Read the eight arms together. abandoned rising with rearmed rising is the healthy shape of a tree the sweep cannot fix: it keeps trying, on an ever-slower schedule, without ever spending unbounded effort. abandoned rising while rearmed stays pinned at zero is the defect this panel exists to catch - the sweep has stopped for the lifetime of the process and no operator-free path returns it, which is exactly the state issue #2783 repaired. undelivered rising is a different statement from either: the touch never reached the leaf, so the tree is neither healed nor proven unhealable and the sweep is being defeated by the very condition it exists to clear (issue #2768) - it belongs on this totals panel rather than the rate panel beside it because the per-consumer cooldown puts repeat touches far apart. healed non-zero at any point is proof the repair path works, so a tree showing healed once and abandoned thereafter is blocked by something that changed, not by something structural. completed is charted here beside healed because the two together separate reachability from repair: completed counts touches that reached the leaf and returned, healed counts pins that subsequently cleared, so completed advancing while healed stays flat is a sweep landing its calls and still failing to clear the block - reachability achieved and not sufficient. unresolvable and faulted sit on this totals panel rather than the rate panel beside it for the same reason abandoned and rearmed do: both are low-cadence by construction, unresolvable because it is a permanent property of a consumer id rather than a retryable condition and faulted because a refundable fault backs off, so a 5 m rate window renders either as a flat zero. orphaned counts blocking pins whose leaf reported no bound tree id, so the leaf was reclaimed or purged and the pin outlived it (issue #3101); the sweep retires the pin rather than reactivating anything. It is charted here because it is a terminal outcome like completed and faulted, and because it is the arm that separates a repair from a vacuous success: before it existed an orphan was reported as completed, so a sweep that could never clear the block looked identical to one that cleared it while the tree's WAL grew without bound. A rate that falls to zero once a deployment drains its backlog is the healthy shape; one that stays non-zero means leaves are still being retired without their pins. Every arm is zero-primed per tree on every GC pass, so a flat zero line is a measured zero and an ABSENT tree means the scheduler never evaluated it at all - a statement about which build is deployed, not about the tree. That reading depends on the arm existing and on its being reachable on the recording path, not on priming alone: three of the then-four terminal arms had no arm of their own before issue #2938, and an armed tag value whose emission site can never execute primes at zero identically (issue #2942).

panels.title: WAL GC starved-leaf checkpoint drive by verdict over range - issue #2692
panels.description: Totals (not a rate) of the six DRIVE arms of orleans.lattice.wal.gc.blocked_leaf_reactivations over the selected range, per tree. This panel answers a question the two panels above it structurally cannot: not whether the sweep REACHED a blocking leaf, but whether reaching it ACHIEVED anything. Until issue #2692 the sweep issued a read-only touch, and the fixture guarding it asserted only that a call had been issued - so a sweep that reached every blocking leaf and cleared none of them was indistinguishable from one that was working, because attempted climbed and healed stayed flat in both cases and nothing anywhere separated them. THE MECHANISM THIS PANEL CHARTS: a leaf that is ALREADY RESIDENT never replays the WAL its partition accrued after activation, because EnsureReplayStarted latches on the replay barrier once activation replay SUCCEEDS - so every later touch short-circuits for the life of that activation, its materialiser checkpoint stays at its sentinel, its durable pin stays unusable, and its tree can never trim. Issue #2871 re-arms the disjoint population whose activation replay FAULTED; neither subsumes the other. That is a REACH argument proven from source, not a statistical one, which is why it holds regardless of how any particular cohort's trees happen to be distributed. The drive makes the sweep actually drive that replay under the same per-silo replay permit gate the activation path uses, so it cannot reintroduce the unbounded-replay pathology of issue #2862 through a side door. drove_lifted = the drive replayed the outstanding WAL, stamped durable snapshot coverage, and left no partition checkpointed without coverage, so the Zero block pin is genuinely gone. drove_no_advance = the drive ran and the pin survived it. drove_memory_refused = the replay was refused under heap pressure, which is a RETRY-WORTHY condition and NOT a verdict on the leaf, so it must not be read as abandonment. drove_not_driven = the grain declined to drive at all, which on a leaf with no tree id means the blocking report and the grain disagree about what is there. drove_already_driving = a drive was already in flight for that leaf, which is sweep CONTENTION rather than leaf starvation and is the arm to read before concluding a tree is being under-served. drove_timed_out = the drive exhausted its StarvationDriveBudget and abandoned its replay rather than keep holding a per-silo replay permit (issue #3065), and IT IS STRUCTURALLY NEAR-SILENT IN THE CASE IT DESCRIBES so it must not be used as the abandonment signal: the scheduler's touch times out at the Orleans response-timeout default long before the drive's five-minute budget elapses, so the verdict is usually recorded by a grain whose caller has already given up and gone to undelivered. Read the abandonment panel below this one instead - that counter is emitted grain-side and does not depend on the caller still being there. READ drove_lifted OVER (drove_lifted + drove_no_advance) AS THE TRUE SUCCESS RATE, and note it is a STRONGER statement than healed: healed is only evidence the sweep is working rather than proof it caused the heal, since ordinary traffic could have reactivated the leaf first, whereas drove_lifted is the sweep's own call returning its own verdict. SUSTAINED drove_no_advance IS THE ALARM AND IT IS SHARPER THAN abandoned: the leaf was reached, its replay ran to completion, and the pin still did not lift, so the residual cause is the snapshot-coverage half rather than reachability. THE LIFTED VERDICT DELIBERATELY REQUIRES BOTH HALVES: advancing the checkpoint alone does NOT lift the pin, because the durable pin for a partition is min(checkpoint, covered) and a starved leaf's coverage is -1 until a snapshot is captured. A drive that claimed lifted on the checkpoint alone would release WAL the leaf cannot actually reconstruct from - silent data loss that looks exactly like the fix working. Every arm is zero-primed per tree on every GC pass, above every early return, so an ABSENT tree means the scheduler never evaluated it at all. A flat zero line carries the weaker claim: priming establishes that the PRIMING path ran, not that the RECORDING path is reachable (issue #2942). A declared-but-never-written arm is frozen at zero, passes every metric gate, and is indistinguishable in a scrape from an arm that is correct and quiet; each of these six arms is witnessed by a test that drives the grain into that verdict, which is the only thing that settles it. This is a totals panel rather than a rate panel for the same reason as the panel beside it: the per-consumer cooldown puts repeat touches far apart, so a 5 m rate window renders them as a flat zero.

panels.title: WAL GC blocking-pin state by tree, partition and status over range - issue #3042
panels.description: Totals (not a rate) of orleans.lattice.wal.gc.blocking_pin_state over the selected range, per tree, partition and status. THE QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: the blocked arm of orleans.lattice.wal.gc.passes says a tree cannot reclaim, but it cannot say whether that is a DEFECT or CORRECT BEHAVIOUR - and those call for opposite responses. The leaf publishes HybridLogicalClock.Zero with offset -1 from a SINGLE branch that covers both routes in, so the durable pin record preserves no difference between them and no amount of reading the pin can recover it (issue #3042). This panel recovers it from the leaf persisted projection checkpoint instead. checkpointed_uncovered = the leaf durably checkpointed that partition, so there IS a WAL offset it could honestly claim, and the unusable pin is the coverage half of min(checkpoint, covered) being absent. THAT IS THE REPAIRABLE STATE and it is the one to act on - BUT ONLY WHEN THE PIN IS ACTUALLY UNUSABLE, which is the premise the whole inference rests on and which this classifier does not measure. checkpointed_coverage_unknown = the leaf durably checkpointed that partition AND its pin sits above the blocking sentinel, so the coverage half was never measured and MUST NOT be assumed absent (issue #3168). Coverage lives in a private per-activation in-memory field that is absent from the persisted state this classifier reads, so it cannot be measured here at all; checkpointed_uncovered is an INFERENCE from unusable AND checkpoint >= 0, valid only where the unusable premise holds. The blocked arm holds it by construction. The floor-holder arm never did - it runs only when NO dormant pin is unusable and samples with no usability filter - so it reported every checkpointed floor holder as repairable and drove a reactivation remedy at every leaf, which then answered that it had no checkpointed-uncovered partition to repair, 4,424 times on one tree. READ checkpointed_coverage_unknown AS AN ABSENCE OF EVIDENCE, NOT AS EVIDENCE OF COVERAGE: it does not say the leaf is covered, only that nothing here measured it, and no instrument yet reports real durable snapshot coverage. never_checkpointed = the leaf holds live data it has never checkpointed, so there is NO offset it could honestly claim; the blocking pin is CORRECT BY DESIGN, no repair exists or should, and a tree blocked only by this arm is not defective - the remedy is to get the leaf to checkpoint, not to change the pin. no_durable_state = the storage provider answered and reported nothing ever persisted for that leaf; it is a FOURTH state and deliberately not folded into never_checkpointed, because folding it there would assert live-data-never-checkpointed on the strength of an ABSENCE, which is exactly the merge this instrument exists to undo. unreadable = the classifier itself could not answer (unparseable consumer id, no storage provider on this silo, or a read that threw); it reports a failure of the MEASUREMENT, not a property of the leaf, and is kept separate so a silo with no provider registered cannot present as an estate of leaves that never persisted anything. READ IT AS: sustained checkpointed_uncovered is an actionable coverage hole; sustained never_checkpointed means the block is correct and the epic premise that it is repairable is wrong; any no_durable_state at all is a finding in its own right and should be escalated rather than aggregated. CLASSIFIED WITHOUT ACTIVATING THE LEAF, which is load-bearing rather than an optimisation: a leaf that could be activated would report a cursor, become present in the registry, and be skipped by the floor before its pin was ever evaluated - so it could not have been the blocker. An instrument that needed the leaf live would measure only leaves that are NOT the problem. The read is charged once per consumer per blocked episode, latched on the consumer budget, so a tree blocked for an hour at the cadence floor pays one read per blocker rather than one per pass. PRIMING IS TWO-LAYER AND BOTH LAYERS MATTER: every tree mints all six arms under the reserved partition value none ONCE PER TREE PER PROCESS, latched on that tree's first collection and not repeated per pass, so an ABSENT series means the classifier is not running on this silo rather than that nothing was classified. That is the ONLY claim a zero prime can carry: Add(0) is idempotent on a counter, so primed-once and primed-ten-thousand-times export the same value and this layer can never say the classifier ran on a GIVEN pass - see orleans.lattice.wal.gc.pass.reach, which advances, for that reading (issue #3075). each classified (tree, partition) then mints all six of its own arms before recording the one that resolved, so a zero on a state reads as measured-and-not-this-state rather than as silence. Filter out partition none to see only real classifications. DIAGNOSTIC ONLY: this value never widens or narrows the trim predicate - a pass reclaims exactly the entries it would have reclaimed had this instrument not existed. This is a totals panel rather than a rate panel because a classification fires once per blocker per episode, so a 5 m rate window renders a genuinely blocked tree as a flat zero. orphaned = the leaf durable state EXISTS but carries NO BOUND TREE ID, so the leaf was reclaimed or purged after the pin was registered and the pin has outlived its publisher (issue #3105); pin registration is birth-gated on a persisted tree id, so a husk is proof the state was cleared afterwards rather than evidence of a leaf not yet born. THIS ARM DID NOT MERELY GO UNREPORTED BEFORE ISSUE #3105 - IT WAS REPORTED AS checkpointed_uncovered, because ClassifyCheckpoint reads only the persisted projection checkpoint offset and a husk retains the last offset it wrote. That is the contradiction to look for when reading this panel against a deployment predating the fix: a tree reporting thousands of REPAIRABLE pins while every repair attempt answered that there was no checkpointed-uncovered partition to repair. The two statements were both produced by this instrument and only one of them was true. An orphan is the only arm actionable WITHOUT DRIVING ANYTHING - there is no leaf left to drive - so it is retired outright by the bulk orphan sweep charted below rather than spending a reactivation attempt and a per-silo replay permit on a leaf that cannot lift it.

panels.title: WAL GC coverage-unknown floor holders by durable offset availability over range - issue #3199
panels.description: Totals (not a rate) of orleans.lattice.wal.gc.coverage_unknown_pin_offset over the selected range, per tree, partition and status. THE QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: the panel above reports checkpointed_coverage_unknown and stops there, but that single arm covers two states with OPPOSITE remedies and no aggregation of that instrument can separate them (issue #3199). A floor-holding pin reaches that arm when the frontier gate declined to claim the checkpoint is uncovered. What happens NEXT depends entirely on whether the same candidate carried a usable durable offset, and blocking_pin_state records the classifier verdict and NOTHING ABOUT THE CANDIDATE THAT PRODUCED IT. Both floor-holder sample lists, the offset-bearing one and the one holding pins that reported no offset, are recorded through the SAME call, so the two cases are byte-identical there. This panel splits them. offset_usable = the candidate durable offset is >= 0. That is the pin population the tree offset floor is a minimum over, so it is the only population issue #3178 liveness drive can admit, and it IS driven when its offset equals that floor. A tree sitting entirely on this arm is latched but NOT stuck: the escape hatch is open and firing. offset_absent = the candidate reported no usable offset. Such a pin constrains no offset floor, so it can NEVER satisfy that equality gate, and the frontier gate has already promoted its state out of the issue #3164 coverage repair. READ A SUSTAINED NON-ZERO offset_absent AS THE TRIPLE EXCLUSION OF ISSUE #3199 ACTUALLY OCCURRING: such a pin is excluded from the blocked arm because its frontier sits above HybridLogicalClock.Zero, from the coverage repair because the frontier gate promoted its state, and from the liveness drive because it carries no offset. The durable pin store merges MONOTONIC MAX on both axes, so the stored frontier is a one-way high-water mark that cannot come back down and NEITHER EXCLUSION CAN BE CLEARED BY ANYTHING THE LEAF SUBSEQUENTLY DOES. That is why this arm is worth a panel of its own rather than a note: it is the difference between a latch that is live but harmless and one that is holding a tree WAL indefinitely with no remedy reachable. BOTH ARMS ARE ZERO-PRIMED PER CLASSIFIED (tree, partition), alongside the blocking_pin_state priming and INDEPENDENTLY OF WHICH STATE RESOLVED, so offset_absent reading zero against a large offset_usable is a MEASURED ABSENCE rather than silence. That is the entire value of this instrument and the property that makes the reading conclusive in EITHER direction: an unprimed zero would be indistinguishable from nothing having been classified, which is precisely the ambiguity that let issue #3158 hide on the one tree its classifier existed to diagnose. THE POPULATION IS EVERY OBSERVATION OF checkpointed_coverage_unknown ANYWHERE, because the promotion that mints that state exists only on the floor-holder path while the blocked arm records the classifier verdict unpromoted. So sum by (tree) here EQUALS blocking_pin_state{status="checkpointed_coverage_unknown"} on the same tree over the same range, and a divergence between the two panels is a DEFECT IN ONE OF THEM rather than a reading about the estate. Cross-check them before drawing any conclusion from this one, but DO NOT WRITE THAT COMPARISON NAIVELY: the equality is an assertion about the recording sites, not about label sets. blocking_pin_state is ALSO primed per collected tree at partition="none", a label this instrument NEVER mints, so you must sum over partition on BOTH sides or the comparison mismatches on EVERY collected tree in the estate. And a tree that never reaches the floor-holder classifier has NO SERIES HERE AT ALL rather than a zero, so guard the absent side explicitly (or vector(0), or scope the comparison to trees where this instrument is present) - an alert without that guard fires on healthy trees. Absence here means "never classified a floor holder", which is NOT the measured zero the priming below guarantees for a tree that did. The arms partition this instrument population exactly, since a candidate durable offset is either negative or it is not. No per-tree reachability priming of its own: whether the floor-holder classifier is wired on this silo is answered by the floor-holder classification panel below, and duplicating that latch here would add a second thing to keep true without adding a discrimination. This is a totals panel rather than a rate panel for the same reason as the panel above, a classification fires once per blocker per episode and a 5 m rate window renders a genuinely latched tree as a flat zero. DIAGNOSTIC ONLY: this value never widens or narrows the trim predicate.

panels.title: WAL GC scheduler phase age - where the silo sweep loop is parked - issue #3060
panels.description: Age, in seconds, of the phase the silo's WAL GC scheduler loop is currently in (orleans.lattice.wal.gc.scheduler.phase_age). THE QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: every other WAL GC series is per tree and is emitted by work the loop performs, so when the loop itself stops they all simply stop changing - which is byte-identical to a healthy silo with nothing to collect. A counter cannot close that gap, because a stopped loop and a quiet one both report a flat line. This is a GAUGE because the failure is a LOCATION problem rather than an EVENT problem: the useful fact is not how many things happened but WHERE the loop is and for HOW LONG. EXACTLY ONE SERIES IS LIVE AT A TIME, the phase the loop is actually in, because a loop is in one phase; publishing a stale age for the ten phases it is not in would leave a reader to pick the live number out of eleven climbing ones and a dashboard to chart ten fictions. That is also why the phase dimension is deliberately NOT zero-primed. It needs no priming: an ObservableGauge reports from its declaration site on every scrape whether or not the scheduler ever ran, which makes this series the BUILD-VERSION WITNESS for the whole six-instrument set - if it is absent the build predates the instruments, and if it is present while the five counters and histograms are not, that is a wiring fault rather than an idle silo. READ IT AS: an age exceeding the cadence the scheduler selected (see the selected-versus-actual panel) is a stalled sweep, and the phase arm names where it stalled. Climbing without bound on collecting.* names the offending tree in the tree tag; on enumerating the tree registry is not answering; on waiting the inter-pass delay itself did not return; a permanent reading on unstarted means ExecuteAsync was never entered, and on disabled means WalGcInterval is set to zero or less, which is a correct exit that on every other instrument is indistinguishable from a wedge. THIS PANEL DOES NOT MEASURE COLLECTION AND MUST NOT BE READ AS DOING SO: it removes the confound that a stopped loop and an idle one look alike, which is a precondition for interpreting the per-tree panels above, not a verdict on them.

panels.title: WAL GC scheduler pass heartbeat (ops/s) - issue #3060
panels.description: Rate at which the silo's WAL GC scheduler loop BEGINS a pass (orleans.lattice.wal.gc.scheduler.passes_started). Counted as a heartbeat ABOVE the tree-registry enumeration, so it advances even on a pass that dies at its first await. That siting is the entire point: the pre-existing orleans.lattice.wal.gc.passes is emitted per tree AFTER enumeration succeeds, so it is structurally silent on exactly the failures that stop the loop, and a loop failing before it reaches any tree produces the same absent series as a loop that is not running. Untagged by tree, because the loop is one per silo and a pass that failed before enumerating has no tree ids to tag with. READ IT AGAINST THE PHASE AGE PANEL: a heartbeat that keeps climbing while every per-tree wal.gc.* series is frozen is a loop that is ALIVE AND FAILING, which needs a different remedy from a loop that has STOPPED - and before this counter existed those two states produced byte-identical scrapes. Zero-primed as the first statement of ExecuteAsync, above the disabled return and above the startup delay, so a flat zero here is a measured zero about a silo that reached the loop, while an absent series means the build lacks the instrument.

panels.title: WAL GC scheduler loop terminations by reason over range - issue #3060
panels.description: Totals (not a rate) of orleans.lattice.wal.gc.scheduler.terminations over the selected range, by reason. A BackgroundService that returns from ExecuteAsync NEVER RUNS AGAIN for the life of the process and the host reports nothing about it, so ANY non-zero value on this panel is a PERMANENT end to silo-wide WAL collection until that silo restarts - this belongs on an alert, not only on a chart. disabled = WalGcInterval is zero or less, a correct exit which on every other instrument in the system is indistinguishable from a wedge. cancelled = an orderly host shutdown, which is not a fault and must not be alerted on. faulted = the loop body threw; it is recorded and then rethrown, so the host's configured exception behaviour is unchanged by the instrumentation. All three arms are zero-primed by WALKING THE ENUM rather than a hand-written list, so a reason added later cannot ship unarmed, and each arm carries a positive control that drives the loop into that termination and observes it advance - which is what makes the zeros the other arms report earned rather than assumed. A totals panel rather than a rate panel because a termination happens at most once per process, and a 5 m rate window renders that single event as a flat zero.

panels.title: WAL GC scheduler enumeration outcome by arm over range - issue #3060
panels.description: Totals (not a rate) of orleans.lattice.wal.gc.scheduler.enumerations over the selected range, by outcome arm. This is the outcome of the tree-registry enumeration that OPENS each pass, and it is the first thing that can go wrong after the loop starts. succeeded = at least one non-blank tree id came back. faulted = the registry threw, which before this instrument existed was swallowed into a debug log and left no trace on any scrape at any level. cancelled = an orderly silo shutdown, not a fault. empty and all_blank ARE DELIBERATELY SEPARATE ARMS: a registry that answers with ids which are all blank REPORTS SUCCESS, RETURNS CONTENT, AND COLLECTS NOTHING, so on every other series in the system it presents exactly as an idle silo, and folding it into empty would hide the one arm that distinguishes a misconfigured registry from a quiet one. timed_out = the scheduler's own bound firing, kept apart from faulted so that A FAILURE OF THE MEASUREMENT IS NEVER REPORTED AS A FAILURE OF THE SUBJECT. All six arms are zero-primed by walking the enum, and each carries a positive control that drives the scheduler into that outcome and observes the arm advance, so a zero on any arm is a measured zero rather than an undriven code path. A totals panel rather than a rate panel because on a healthy silo every arm but succeeded is expected to read zero for the life of the process, and a rate window renders the rare event that matters as a flat line.

panels.title: WAL GC scheduler selected wait versus actual pass duration (p95) - issue #3060
panels.description: The two halves of the scheduler's cadence, charted together because NEITHER IS INTERPRETABLE ALONE. orleans.lattice.wal.gc.scheduler.wait is the interval the loop CHOSE before its next pass, observed once per pass at the delay site so it is recorded even when the pass reached no tree. orleans.lattice.wal.gc.scheduler.pass_duration is how long a pass ACTUALLY took, recorded in a finally so a pass that faults, is cancelled, or is abandoned at a bound is measured too - that population's duration is itself the diagnosis, and siting the record on the success path would discard exactly the sample worth having. WHY BOTH: the wait is sited on the scheduler's DECISION and therefore cannot observe anything that happens AFTER the decision. A silo whose per-tree touches all end at the Orleans default 30 s response timeout selects the interval floor on every pass while the wall period is twice that, so the wait reads a flat, healthy-looking floor throughout and the stretch is invisible on it. DIVERGENCE BETWEEN THE TWO SERIES IS THE SIGNATURE of a loop whose passes are being stretched by something the cadence policy never saw. Read the wait's own shape as well: the adaptive cadence returns to the configured minimum ONLY after a fully successful pass, so every other exit relaxes geometrically toward the ceiling, and that climbing ladder is the one POSITIVE signature an alive-but-failing loop emits - every other series such a loop touches is frozen exactly as a stopped loop leaves them. Neither histogram is zero-primed, deliberately: the empty state of a duration distribution is UNDEFINED rather than zero, and a primed 0 s sample would corrupt every quantile on this panel. Their liveness is anchored instead to the pass heartbeat, with exactly one observation per started pass asserted by fixture - and that anchor is checkable directly from a scrape, because the _count series is emitted even where bucket series are not. THE MEAN TARGETS ARE THE ONES THAT RENDER EVERYWHERE. Measured against the deployment scrape this issue was raised from: that exporter emits NO histogram bucket series at all (zero _bucket series and zero histogram TYPE declarations across 16089 scraped lines), so every quantile target in this bundle is empty there and only the _sum over _count mean is readable. The p95 targets are kept for deployments whose exporter does emit buckets, and are labelled so an empty line is not misread as a dead instrument.

targets.legendFormat: actual pass duration p95 (bucket exporters only)

panels.title: WAL GC starvation-drive abandonments by tree over range - issue #3065
panels.description: Totals (not a rate) of orleans.lattice.wal.replay.starvation_drive_abandonments over the selected range, per tree. THIS IS THE SOLE DISCRIMINATOR BETWEEN A BOUNDED-BUT-SLOW DRIVE AND A DRIVE THAT WOULD HAVE PARKED FOREVER, and reading it is not optional when the reactivation panels above look frozen. WHY IT HAD TO EXIST: before issue #3065 the starvation drive acquired a permit on the per-silo WAL replay concurrency gate and then passed CancellationToken.None to every await inside the permit-guarded region, so a drive whose commit-log read never returned held one of two permits indefinitely and could not even be cancelled. The gate drained, every leaf activation on the silo queued behind it, and the estate presented as an activation outage with no instrument anywhere naming the cause. Bounding the drive fixes that and NECESSARILY DESTROYS THE DIAGNOSTIC THAT FOUND IT. The frozen signature on two independently frozen production containers was attempted 81 = undelivered 78 + completed 3, with all three completions returning AlreadyDriving because they bounced off an in-flight latch a predecessor never cleared. A drive that is merely SLOW now reproduces that shape byte for byte: the scheduler's touch still times out at the Orleans response-timeout default long before the drive's five-minute budget elapses, so it still records undelivered, and successors still bounce off the latch, so they still record drove_already_driving. NONE OF THE SCHEDULER'S ARMS CAN SEPARATE THE TWO ANY MORE. Only this counter can, because it is emitted GRAIN-SIDE as the drive gives up and therefore does not depend on the caller still being there to observe anything - which is exactly why the drove_timed_out verdict arm on the panel above is not a substitute for it. READ IT AS: advancing means drives are reaching their budget and the remedy is UPSTREAM OF LATTICE, in the host-supplied commit-log storage whose read is not returning - Lattice's own defect was that the call was unbounded, and that is now fixed regardless of why the provider blocked. Flat at zero means drives are completing and a frozen-looking reactivation panel is ordinary sweep contention, not a wedged gate. PRIMED AT ZERO BESIDE THE attempted ARM ON THE SCHEDULER, deliberately NOT at the grain's drive entry point: priming at the drive would make an absent series mean no drive has ever run as well as this build is not deployed, which is precisely the ambiguity the priming exists to remove. Co-primed with attempted the reading is unambiguous - attempted above zero WITH this series present is a real measured zero, attempted above zero WITH this series absent proves the build carrying the fix never landed - so the prime doubles as a free deployment proof. ONE ARM COVERS BOTH ABANDONMENT SHAPES, a drive that timed out while queued for a permit and one that timed out deep inside the replay, because both call for the same response; they stay separable when it matters, since only the first also records on the canceled arm of orleans.lattice.wal.replay.permit_queue_wait. The drive's elapsed time is on the paired warning log rather than as a histogram, because an abandoned drive's duration is approximately the budget by construction. Tagged by tree plus the universal derived tenant dimension, which the leaf grain resolves from the same tree id the scheduler does, so the zero primed on the scheduler and the count recorded by the grain are one series. This is a totals panel rather than a rate panel for the same reason as the panels above it - abandonments are rare and far apart, so a 5 m rate window renders a genuinely abandoning silo as a flat zero.

panels.title: WAL GC scheduler-wide backoff by cause (p95, s) - issue #3064
panels.description: The backoff the WAL garbage-collection scheduler is currently sitting on (orleans.lattice.wal.gc.scheduler_backoff), per cause. THE QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: is WAL GC asleep, or is it dead? Nothing else on this dashboard can tell you. A pass that collects nothing writes no per-tree series at all, so orleans.lattice.wal.gc.passes, orleans.lattice.wal.gc.interval and the backlog panels all simply STOP - identically - whether the scheduler has backed off by design or has stopped running. A live container was scraped five times over twenty minutes and recorded not one wal.gc.interval while leaf activation was demonstrably healthy, and the scrape could not settle which of the two had happened; that ambiguity cost this investigation days (issue #3064). This panel is the missing witness. NOTE IT IS NOT THE SAME QUANTITY as the WAL GC adaptive interval panel above: that one is ONE TREE's cadence and is tagged by tree, this one is the WHOLE SCHEDULER's retry wait before it has any tree to speak of, so it is silo-scoped, carries the platform tenant sentinel, and has no tree tag - do not filter it by $tree and do not read the two as the same series at different resolutions. THE CAUSE ARMS ARE THE POINT and they are not interchangeable. scheduled = the registry was enumerated and an ordinary per-tree cadence was selected; no scheduler-wide backoff is in force and the floor is reported, so this arm is the healthy baseline. empty = the enumeration SUCCEEDED and found no collectable tree; that is a correct observation of an idle silo rather than a fault, so it relaxes all the way to LatticeOptions.WalGcInterval and is not an alarm. faulted = the enumeration THREW, so the pass learned nothing at all; the wait it then picks IS the operator's blindness window, because the scheduler cannot notice the fault clearing until it next tries. The faulted ladder is therefore capped far lower, at the reactivation block age clamped into the configured band, which is why the two ladders have DISJOINT RANGES above that cap: a reading above the fault ceiling can only be empty, so a high value is self-identifying before the tag is read. RECORDED UNCONDITIONALLY ON EVERY PASS AND EVERY PATH, including the first pass and including a silo with no trees, which is load-bearing rather than incidental: this panel deliberately OMITS the 'or vector(0)' fallback its neighbours use, so a flat reading is a MEASURED reading and 'No data' means THE BUILD CARRYING THIS INSTRUMENT IS NOT DEPLOYED - read it against the WAL GC adaptive interval panel above, whose instrument is known to fire, and treat interval-present-with-backoff-absent as proof of a stale deployment rather than of a healthy scheduler. Priming it on the fault path instead would have made an absent series mean either 'nothing has gone wrong' or 'not deployed', and this epic confused exactly those two more than once. It cannot share the per-tree interval site either, because that site is silent on precisely the zero-tree silo that most needs a liveness witness.

panels.title: WAL GC consecutive registry-enumeration faults (p95) - issue #3064
panels.description: Length of the CURRENT run of consecutive failed WAL garbage-collection registry enumerations (orleans.lattice.wal.gc.scheduler_consecutive_faults), per cause. Read it BESIDE the scheduler-backoff panel, which says how long the scheduler will wait but not how deep the hole is. It is a CURRENT STREAK, not a lifetime total, which is why it can fall: the first pass whose enumeration succeeds resets it to zero, and a success here means only that the registry ANSWERED - a pass that read the registry and found no tree resets it just as a pass that found fifty does, because answering is the entire thing this series measures. A streak that keeps returning to zero is a scheduler absorbing transients and needs no action; one that only climbs is a registry the scheduler cannot read at all, and that is the operator-actionable state, because the enumeration is a full key-range scan across every shard of the tree registry and is therefore the first thing to fail when leaf activation is saturated (issue #2368). Recorded at the same unconditional per-pass site as the backoff series and carrying the same cause tag, so the same priming argument applies verbatim and this panel likewise omits the 'or vector(0)' fallback: a flat zero is a MEASURED zero meaning the last enumeration succeeded, and 'No data' is a statement about the DEPLOYMENT rather than about the registry. A zero does NOT mean WAL GC is reclaiming anything - an enumeration that succeeds and yields nothing collectable is a success by this measure, and the pass-outcome panel is what answers that question.

panels.title: WAL GC pass and tree reachability by stage over range - issue #3075
panels.description: Totals (not a rate) of orleans.lattice.wal.gc.pass.reach and orleans.lattice.wal.gc.tree.reach over the selected range, by stage. THE QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: orleans.lattice.wal.gc.passes and orleans.lattice.wal.gc.interval are both recorded INSIDE the per-tree collection, which a pass reaches only after clearing several earlier exits - so when one of those exits is taken they do not advance, and a flat series is indistinguishable from a silo that was never scheduled at all. The usual remedy, siting the instrument outside the failing region, is UNAVAILABLE here because the quantity being counted only exists inside it. This layer is what is available instead: an arm above every exit, so a flat downstream series can be read as MEASURED rather than as NEVER-EXECUTED (issue #3075). THE LAYER IS TWO INSTRUMENTS AND THAT IS DELIBERATE. A pass spans the whole tree registry, so it belongs to no tenant and wal.gc.pass.reach carries the platform sentinel; a tree visit belongs to the tenant owning the tree, so wal.gc.tree.reach is tenant-derived exactly like wal.gc.passes and wal.gc.interval. Carrying both under one instrument would split its series across two attribution rules, and a tenant-scoped query would then return the per-tree arms while silently dropping the pass-level ones - which are precisely the arms that answer whether the scheduler ran at all. DO NOT ADD A tree OR tenant FILTER TO QUERY A. The pass-level arms deliberately carry the reserved tree value _none_ and the platform tenant, because two of the exits are the catch arms of the registry enumeration itself - obtaining the tree list is the operation that failed, so no tree id exists to label them with and none ever can. Either filter would hide exactly the arms that answer is the scheduler running at all. QUERY A STAGES: pass_entered is the denominator, taken as the first statement of a pass; registry_cancelled, registry_failed, registry_timed_out, loop_cancelled, no_due_tree, pass_completed_immediate and pass_completed_scheduled are the seven terminating exits, and at quiescence they SUM TO pass_entered - while a pass is in flight the entry arm legitimately leads the exit arms by the number of passes running, so the production reading is 0 <= entered - sum(exits) <= passes in flight and an equality alert would flap once per pass and be muted. pass_completed_immediate means the next tree was already due when the pass ended, i.e. the scheduler is running flat out, which is an operational signal in its own right and is why it is not folded into pass_completed_scheduled. QUERY B STAGES: tree_seen and tree_collected carry a real tree and are a PAIR - neither half is interpretable alone. The difference between them is the set skipped by the not-yet-due check, which is the HEALTHY MAJORITY on any given pass rather than a fault, so a large gap is expected and a zero gap on a many-tree silo is the anomaly. NEVER SUM QUERY A AND QUERY B: they count different populations under different attribution rules. THIS LAYER ADVANCES RATHER THAN PRIMING A ZERO, and that is the whole design: the construction it generalises (the partition=none layer of issue #3042) mints zeros, and Add(0) is idempotent on a counter, so a series primed once and a series primed ten thousand times are byte-identical and no sample count exists to separate them. Priming can establish that a region was reached AT LEAST ONCE and nothing more - which makes a priming layer an instance of the very defect class it was prescribed to cure, a series that exists and does not advance. Read rates here, not just totals, for that reason. DIAGNOSTIC ONLY: this instrument never changes what a pass is allowed to trim, and it does not change what any existing WAL GC instrument counts.

panels.title: WAL GC bulk orphan-pin sweep by status over range - issue #3105
panels.description: Totals (not a rate) of orleans.lattice.wal.gc.orphan_pin_sweep over the selected range, per tree and status (issue #3105). THE QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: how many durable materialiser pins does this tree actually hold, and how many of them are orphans? NO OTHER SERIES CAN SAY. The cursor floor's blocking report is capped at MaxReportedBlockingConsumers = 8, so the blocking-pin-state panel above charts at most eight consumers however many thousands are there - and the sweep that retired them was bounded the same way, at four touches per pass behind a five-minute minimum block age, because every one of its bounds was sized for a handful of LIVE BUT STUCK leaves rather than for a backlog of DEAD ones. The measured drain was 63 pins an hour against 9,468 pins: six days, during which the offset floor - a MIN over all pins - trims nothing at all and the WAL grows without bound. The arms of this instrument PARTITION the examined population, so sum by (tree) over one sweep is the tree's whole durable pin count. retired = the leaf state carries no bound tree id and the pin was removed from every shard key it was found under. deferred = the same finding, left in place because the pass's retirement budget was already spent. live = the leaf still carries a bound tree id, which the sweep NEVER touches, because a live leaf's pin is retention the WAL GC is obliged to honour. unresolved = the consumer id did not parse back to a leaf grain id, so no leaf could be read and no claim was made. unreadable = the leaf-state read failed, and THE SWEEP FAILS CLOSED ON IT: an unreadable leaf is never retired, because retiring a pin whose leaf might still be live would authorise a trim over a prefix that leaf has not replayed - silent data loss that looks exactly like the fix working.
