DEFERRED IS THE BACKLOG SIGNAL AND IS DELIBERATELY A COUNTER ARM RATHER THAN A GAUGE: a sustained non-zero deferred rate means orphans remain and the sweep is still draining them, while deferred at zero with retired no longer advancing means the backlog is gone. That reads the operational question off an advancing series and carries none of the declaration-order hazards an observable gauge would bring with it. THE ABSENCE OF ANY SUCH SIGNAL IS WHAT LET ISSUE #3105 RUN UNDETECTED FOR DAYS: the only orphan series in existence was the reactivation sweep's monotonically advancing orphaned arm, on which a 63-per-hour drain against a 9,468-pin backlog is indistinguishable from steady healthy progress - the counter rises either way and nothing anywhere carries the denominator. READ IT WITH wal.gc.passes{outcome="reclaimed"} BESIDE IT: retired climbing is the sweep working, but only reclaimed turning non-zero proves the floor actually moved as a result. Every arm is zero-primed per tree, so a flat zero is a measured zero and an absent tree means the scheduler never evaluated it.

panels.title: WAL GC floor-holder classification coverage over range - issue #3158
panels.description: Totals (not a rate) of orleans.lattice.wal.gc.floor_holder_classification over the selected range, per tree and status (issue #3158). THE QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: of this tree's durable materialiser pins, how many did the floor-holder classification actually look at? READ IT WITH THE BLOCKING-PIN-STATE PANEL ABOVE, ALWAYS - it is the denominator that instrument has never carried, and without it that panel cannot distinguish two opposite conditions. Five zero status arms on a tree NOTHING EVER CLASSIFIED are byte-identical to five measured zeroes on a tree that WAS classified and found nothing in a notable state. On the live estate that ambiguity went unread for the entire life of a tree carrying 1.07 GiB of WAL that reclaimed nothing: its five blocking_pin_state arms sat at zero under the reserved partition value none - the signature of priming at registration and not one measurement since - and were taken to mean no pin was in a notable state, when they meant NO PIN WAS EVER LOOKED AT. The cause was structural rather than operational: the classifier had exactly one call site, on the floor-blocked heal path, and its input was derived from the floor-blocked report. A tree classified over_ceiling produces no such report, so the classifier was never called for it AND would have iterated an empty list if it had been - which is why hoisting the call alone would have changed nothing while looking entirely correct. The candidates now come from the sweep's own enumeration of the durable pin store, which owes the report nothing. THE TWO ARMS PARTITION THE ENUMERATED POPULATION, so sum by (tree) over one sweep is the tree's whole durable pin count and classified / sum is the coverage fraction outright. classified = a pin whose leaf state was read and whose result was recorded on blocking_pin_state. unclassified = a pin the sample did not reach. A TINY CLASSIFIED FRACTION IS THE DESIGNED BEHAVIOUR AND NOT AN ALARM: every classification is a durable storage read, one live tree was measured at 52,224 pins on a single sweep, and classifying a population would turn a diagnostic into a storage-read storm on a tree that is already unhealthy - so the sample is capped per sweep by a constant independent of how many pins the tree holds. THE SAMPLE IS NOT ARBITRARY: the durable materialiser offset floor is a MIN over every pin, so the pins carrying the lowest frontier are the ones actually holding it, and those are the ones sampled, in ascending frontier order with ties broken on the consumer id so the reported holders are stable across scrapes rather than churning with dictionary order on a tree whose pins all sit at HybridLogicalClock.Zero. Both arms are zero-primed per tree above every early return, so a flat zero is a measured zero and an absent tree means the classification is not wired on this silo.

panels.title: WAL compactions by trigger over range - issue #3107
panels.description: Totals (not a rate) of orleans.lattice.wal.compactions over the selected range, per tree, SHARD and trigger (issues #3107, #3206). THE QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: is the WAL actually RETURNING the space its garbage collector trims? TRIMMING DOES NOT FREE DISK ON A LOG-STRUCTURED PROVIDER. A trim marks entries dead and appends a trim marker; only a COMPACTION - a rewrite of the surviving entries into a fresh file - returns the bytes, and until issue #3107 no series anywhere said whether that rewrite was happening. MEASURED ON A LIVE CONTAINER: a tree trimmed 113,675 entries over 55 minutes while its WAL GREW by 1.1 MB, and orleans.lattice.wal.entries_trimmed charted that as healthy progress because it counts ENTRIES, never BYTES. THE DISCRIMINATOR MUST BE READ PER SHARD, NOT PER TREE. Every compaction trigger is SHARD-LOCAL: the ratio test compares one shard's dead bytes against its own payload, so a tree-scoped sum averages one threshold test per shard and reports a dead fraction that no shard actually holds. That is not a coarser version of the right answer, it is a different and wrong one - an ACTIVE MINORITY OF SHARDS KEEPS THE TREE COUNTERS ADVANCING WHILE A STRANDED MAJORITY OF THE BYTES NEVER MOVES, and at tree scope the healthy shape and the fault shape are identical. MEASURED ON A LIVE CONTAINER FOR #3206: three of eight shards holding 81% of a 1.6 GB WAL had never compacted while the tree reported 21 compactions and 1.57 GB reclaimed. READ IT PER SHARD AGAINST orleans.lattice.wal.entries_trimmed, which is shard-tagged for the same reason: sustained trimming on a shard whose compaction arms are flat means that shard's dead bytes are accumulating and its thresholds are not being reached. THE TRIGGER ARMS ARE THE COMPLETE SET OF PATHS THAT CAN REWRITE A SHARD. ratio = dead bytes reached CompactionThreshold as a FRACTION of the file (the historical and only pre-#3107 trigger), which is well amortised - at the 0.5 default it writes about one live byte per dead byte reclaimed - but is UNBOUNDED IN ABSOLUTE TERMS: a shard that stalls at a dead fraction of 0.49 strands that space indefinitely however many gigabytes it is, which is exactly what the measurement above caught at a dead fraction of 0.08 on 11.7 GB. ceiling = dead bytes reached the ABSOLUTE CompactionMaximumDeadBytes cap added by #3107. reconcile = an unconditional compaction at shard activation, which never fires for an actively-written tree because its WAL grain does not deactivate. A FLAT ceiling ARM IS CORRECT, NOT A FAULT: CompactionMaximumDeadBytes defaults to 0 (disabled), because compaction rewrites every LIVE byte to reclaim the DEAD ones, so cost per byte reclaimed is live/dead and an absolute cap far below the live size raises write amplification without bound. Enabling it by default would be a silent I/O regression on every existing deployment, so it is opt-in and this arm stays at a measured zero until an operator sets the cap. EVERY ARM IS ZERO-PRIMED PER SHARD when that shard first loads, so a flat zero is a MEASURED zero rather than an unpublished series - the distinction that mattered in #3107, where 'this WAL has never reclaimed a byte' and 'this deployment does not run the file provider' both rendered as no-data, and that #3206 restored at shard scope, where an unprimed shard tag would leave 'this shard has never compacted' indistinguishable from 'this shard is not reporting'. SCOPE: emitted by the FILE WAL provider only. A deployment on a backend whose trim deletes rows outright carries no dead bytes and needs no compaction, so an absent series there is correct.

panels.title: WAL bytes reclaimed by compaction over range - issues #3107, #3206
panels.description: Totals (not a rate) of orleans.lattice.wal.compaction.reclaimed_bytes over the selected range, per tree and SHARD (issues #3107, #3206). The BYTES half of the compaction pair above, which counts EVENTS: a shard can compact regularly and still reclaim almost nothing, and only this panel separates the two. DELIBERATELY A MONOTONIC COUNTER RATHER THAN A GAUGE OF CURRENT DEAD BYTES. A gauge of that kind needs a compensating write on every trim, and issue #2700 established on this repository that a compensating write which can be lost - to a disposed shard, a re-created provider, or a torn activation - RATCHETS THE SERIES PERMANENTLY, leaving real waste indistinguishable from accumulated drift, which is the exact question the instrument exists to answer. FOR PRESENT-TRUTH OCCUPANCY READ ILattice.GetStorageUsageAsync's WalPhysicalBytes INSTEAD, which is derived per sample from the shard's write position and so cannot drift. That field is also what the WalMaxRetainedBytes ceiling now compares against: before #3107 the ceiling was compared to the LOGICAL retained total, which omits dead bytes, so a WAL could legitimately occupy approaching TWICE its configured ceiling without ever reporting a breach. READ IT AGAINST THE PANEL ABOVE, AND READ BOTH PER SHARD: for a GIVEN SHARD, compactions advancing with this flat means that shard's rewrites are finding nothing to reclaim; both advancing together is the healthy shape; trimming with both flat is the #3107 condition. THE PER-SHARD QUALIFIER IS LOAD-BEARING, NOT PEDANTRY. Compaction is decided per shard, so the same three-way discriminator applied to a tree-scoped sum is UNSOUND: an active minority of shards keeps both series advancing while a stranded majority of the bytes never moves, and the fault renders exactly like the healthy shape. That is issue #3206, measured on a live container as three of eight shards holding 81% of a 1.6 GB WAL having never compacted while the tree reported 21 compactions and 1.57 GB reclaimed. Zero-primed per SHARD alongside orleans.lattice.wal.compactions, so a flat zero here is likewise measured rather than absent, and a missing shard series means that shard is not reporting rather than that it has reclaimed nothing.

panels.title: WAL compaction gate inputs - bytes per shard - issue #3206
panels.description: The two byte inputs the file provider compaction gate actually tests, sampled per SHARD at every evaluation whether or not that evaluation decided to compact (orleans.lattice.wal.compaction.eval.retained_bytes and orleans.lattice.wal.compaction.eval.dead_bytes, issue #3206). THE QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: when a shard compaction arms are flat, is that shard below its threshold or is the gate never being reached at all? The two compaction panels above count OUTCOMES, so a flat shard is silent about its cause: a shard sitting at a dead fraction of 0.49 and a shard whose gate is never evaluated render identically. These series are recorded at the TOP of the evaluation, before any arm is tested, so a shard that never compacts still reports the numbers it declined on. THE RATIO CHARTED HERE IS THE ONE THE GATE ITSELF TESTS, EXACTLY. dead / (retained + dead) is the fraction compared against CompactionThreshold, and dead alone is the figure compared against CompactionMaximumDeadBytes, so an operator can reproduce both decisions from outside the process rather than inferring them. WHY THIS IS NOT DERIVABLE FROM THE STORAGE-USAGE FIELDS: WalPhysicalBytes counts FRAMED records while the retained figure counts PAYLOAD, so a physical-minus-retained subtraction yields dead PLUS the per-record framing overhead, in both the numerator and the denominator of the ratio, and is therefore strictly an UPPER BOUND on the fraction the gate tests rather than the fraction itself. On the live estate that bound spanned 29% to 53% around a 0.5 threshold, which straddles it and does not decide the question. READ IT WITH THE ENTRY-COUNT PANEL BESIDE IT, which supplies the divisor that turns these bytes into a mean payload and makes the framing term computable. ALWAYS READ PER SHARD: the gate is shard-local, so a tree-scoped sum averages one threshold test per shard and reports a dead fraction that no shard holds. Armed per shard at load from true post-recovery state, so an absent shard series means that shard is not reporting rather than that it holds nothing.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, tree, shard) (rate(orleans_lattice_wal_compaction_eval_retained_bytes_bucket{tree=~"$tree",cluster=~"$cluster",instance=~"$silo"}[5m]))) or vector(0)
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, tree, shard) (rate(orleans_lattice_wal_compaction_eval_dead_bytes_bucket{tree=~"$tree",cluster=~"$cluster",instance=~"$silo"}[5m]))) or vector(0)

panels.title: WAL compaction gate inputs - entries per shard - issue #3206
panels.description: The retained and dead ENTRY COUNTS behind the byte panel beside this one, sampled per SHARD at every compaction evaluation (orleans.lattice.wal.compaction.eval.retained_entries and orleans.lattice.wal.compaction.eval.dead_entries, issue #3206). THE QUESTION THIS ANSWERS: what is the mean payload on this shard, and therefore how large is the per-record framing term that separates the bytes the gate tests from the bytes the file occupies? Dividing the byte series beside this one by these counts gives mean payload per shard directly; the framing overhead per record is a known constant of FileWalRecordFormat, so the count multiplied by that constant is the framing term outright. WITHOUT THIS PANEL THE CORRECTION IS NOT MERELY UNKNOWN, IT IS UNBOUNDED IN THE DIRECTION THAT MATTERS: the same subtraction error is about 0.4% at a 4 KB mean payload and about 6.2% at 256 B, and those two answers fork the remedy, because one says the gate is working and the shard is simply below threshold while the other says the shard is stranded above it. THE COUNTS ARE ALSO THE HONEST DENOMINATOR FOR orleans.lattice.wal.entries_trimmed, which is now shard-tagged for the same reason: sustained trimming on a shard whose dead entries are climbing and whose compaction arms are flat is dead backlog accumulating with no rewrite in sight, which is the #3206 condition stated in the units the gate does not use. ALWAYS READ PER SHARD. Armed per shard at load, so a flat series is measured rather than absent.

targets.expr: histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, tree, shard) (rate(orleans_lattice_wal_compaction_eval_retained_entries_bucket{tree=~"$tree",cluster=~"$cluster",instance=~"$silo"}[5m]))) or vector(0)
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, tree, shard) (rate(orleans_lattice_wal_compaction_eval_dead_entries_bucket{tree=~"$tree",cluster=~"$cluster",instance=~"$silo"}[5m]))) or vector(0)

panels.title: WAL GC trim stops by reason (ops/s) - issue #3149
panels.description: Rate of WAL garbage-collection shard scans by the reason each scan stopped (orleans.lattice.wal.gc.trim_stop), per tree (issues #3149, #3155). THIS IS THE PANEL THAT MAKES A ZERO-RECLAIM PASS ATTRIBUTABLE. The pass-outcome panel classifies a pass over_ceiling whenever the tree is above its byte ceiling, and that classification is decided by the CONSUMER-CURSOR floor alone - so a tree stranded by the DURABLE LEAF-CHECKPOINT OFFSET FLOOR reports an available cursor floor, reclaims zero on every pass, grows without bound, and over_ceiling is also the one outcome on which the blocking-pin diagnostic is never written. Six arms: exhausted (the scan consumed the whole shard - healthy) and empty (the shard holds no entries, which is NOT the same as having just reclaimed everything and must not be averaged into it); against offset_floor (the first entry examined sat above the durable checkpoint floor, so ONE LAGGING LEAF IS HOLDING THE WHOLE TREE, that floor being a minimum over reported checkpoints), cursor_floor (neither the consumer cursor nor the TTL ceiling accepted the entry, which indicts a LAGGING CONSUMER CURSOR), causal_frontier (a reported per-origin stable frontier does not dominate the entry vector clock, which indicts a REPLICATION ORIGIN rather than the consumer that reported it) and block_pin (a consumer buffer pin holds the entry back - a deliberate hold rather than a lag, so a sustained run against a consumer that is no longer buffering is a LEAKED PIN). Those last three were one not_eligible arm until issue #3155 split them, which left a tree provably stranded with no way to say by what. One measurement per shard per pass, so a single stranded partition stays visible rather than being absorbed by its healthy siblings. READ IT WITH THE PASS-OUTCOME PANEL: a sustained offset_floor rate alongside over_ceiling passes is unbounded WAL growth with a named cause. Every arm - exhausted, empty, offset_floor, cursor_floor, causal_frontier and block_pin - is zero-primed above every early return, which is why this query omits the or-vector-zero fallback used elsewhere on this dashboard: fabricating a zero would reintroduce the false zero the priming exists to remove, and here an absent series genuinely means WAL GC is not running for that tree on the selected silo.

panels.title: WAL GC ceiling unsatisfiable (ops/s) - issue #3242
panels.description: Rate of WAL garbage-collection passes that found the tree's configured WalMaxRetainedBytes ARITHMETICALLY UNREACHABLE against the live set the pass just measured - below LatticeOptions.WalMaxRetainedBytesWorkingSetMultiple (2) times the logical retained payload (orleans.lattice.wal.gc.ceiling_unsatisfiable, issue #3242). THIS PANEL NAMES A CONFIGURATION FAULT, NOT A LAG, AND THAT DISTINCTION IS THE WHOLE POINT. The pass-outcome panel's stranded and over_ceiling arms both say bytes could not be reclaimed, which an operator reads as a lagging consumer or a pinned floor and acts on by chasing the consumer. A tree on this panel is telling you the opposite: nothing is lagging, the tree is simply larger than its own ceiling permits a healthy tree to be, and no amount of reclamation can bring it inside - so the remedy is to raise the ceiling or shrink the tree, and chasing consumers is wasted effort. Before this series the two rendered identically. WHY TWO TIMES: a log-structured provider reclaims dead bytes only by rewriting a segment, and rewrites once dead bytes reach a configured fraction t of total payload, so designed steady-state occupancy peaks at live/(1-t) - twice the live set at the file provider's default 0.5 ratio - and the ceiling has been compared against PHYSICAL occupancy since issue #3107. A ceiling below that multiple is breached by a tree doing nothing wrong, and because WalBytePressureReclaimTarget (0.8) puts the disarm point below the natural floor of the same compaction cycle, it is breached PERMANENTLY: the advisory byte-pressure alarm arms and can never clear, which destroys its ability to distinguish pathological growth from normal size. DELIBERATELY NOT AN ARM OF THE PASS-OUTCOME COUNTER: those arms partition invocations, whereas this condition co-occurs with reclaimed, over_ceiling and stranded alike, so an arm would have stolen invocations from whichever arm names them today and an operator alerting on stranded would have watched it fall silent as the condition worsened. READ IT AGAINST THE PASS-OUTCOME PANEL: every pass on an affected tree agrees, because this is a standing property of the configuration rather than an event, so the rate here tracks that tree's pass rate.
